facts.fact: Philanthropist Edith Hooper commissioned the house, which Marcel Breuer designed with Herbert Beckhard.
facts.quote: It was commissioned by philanthropist Edith Hooper, and designed by architects Marcel Breuer and Herbert Beckhard.

facts.fact: Ground was broken in 1958 and the house was finished in 1959.
facts.quote: Ground was broken on the project in 1958 and the house was completed in 1959.

facts.fact: It is a 'binuclear' plan: a central courtyard separates living and entertaining areas from the family and bedroom areas.
facts.quote: A central courtyard divides the house into living/dining/cooking/entertaining and family/bedroom areas.

facts.fact: The front door faces the courtyard, and glass doors plus an opening in the stone rear wall frame a view straight through the house to Lake Roland.
facts.quote: The front door faces the center of the courtyard, where glass doors and a large rectangular opening in the stone of the rear wall frame an unobstructed view literally through the home and to Lake Roland to the east.

facts.fact: The separate wings let guests be entertained without disturbing bedrooms, and thick stone walls help control noise.
facts.quote: The impressive noise management is enhanced by the thick stone walls, one of which is on the side of the family wing facing the courtyard, broken only by a relatively narrow doorway to the front entry hall.

facts.fact: Most rooms sit on the periphery with a full wall of glass, much of it floor-to-ceiling sliding doors.
facts.quote: Every room except for the bathrooms, the "family room", and the kitchen are located along the home's periphery and therefore have an entire wall that is made of glass, half of which is a floor to ceiling sliding-glass door.

facts.fact: The lake side is glazed while the west side is a long, nearly featureless wall of Maryland fieldstone.
facts.quote: Many images of the home are taken from this perspective, as this side of the house faces the lake and is covered in glass, while the west wall is a long wall of Maryland fieldstone, broken only by the front door and otherwise relatively featureless.

facts.fact: The Oficina theatre company was founded in 1958 at the Law School of the University of São Paulo.
facts.quote: Teat(r)o Oficina Uzyna Uzona or simply Teatro Oficina (English: Oficina Theater), is a theater company based in the neighborhood of Bixiga, in the Brazilian city of São Paulo. It was founded in 1958 at the Law School of the University of São Paulo by Amir Haddad, José Celso Martinez Correa, Carlos Queiroz Telles and Ron Daniels.

facts.fact: A fire destroyed the company's earlier headquarters in 1966, and plays were staged to raise funds to restore the building.
facts.quote: In 1966, the company's headquarters was destroyed by a fire. Remounts of plays were staged to raise funds and restore the building.

facts.fact: The current building was designed by Lina Bo Bardi and Edson Elito and inaugurated in 1994.
facts.quote: The current building was designed in 1984 by Lina Bo Bardi and Edson Elito and inaugurated in 1994.

facts.fact: The Guardian chose it in 2015 as the best theatre in the world for architectural design.
facts.quote: In 2015, it was chosen by The Guardian as the best theater in the world in the architectural design category.

facts.fact: The renovation added a long central walkway and side galleries over four levels, so spectators have different points of view.
facts.quote: The renovation included a central walkway 1.5 meters wide and 50 meters long, and front and back accesses.

facts.fact: The design uses iron scaffolding, an exposed brick structure, internal plant beds and a large window.
facts.quote: The extended design with iron scaffolding, an exposed brick structure, internal plant beds, a large window and the stage-platform connection represent the start of a new phase for the company.

facts.fact: The building is listed as heritage and has been in a long dispute over towers planned on the neighbouring land.
facts.quote: Since the 1980s, Teatro Oficina has been involved in a dispute with Grupo Silvio Santos, which intends to build residential towers on the land next to the venue.

facts.fact: Jørn Utzon designed the housing complex for Danes who had worked abroad for long periods.
facts.quote: The houses were designed by Jørn Utzon for Danes who have worked for long periods abroad.

facts.fact: The scheme grew from a 1953 competition project, inspired by traditional Danish farmhouses around a courtyard and by Chinese architecture, with houses opening to a central court but protected from outside by their outer wall.
facts.quote: The 63 units were based on a competition project Utzon had developed for the south of Sweden in 1953, inspired by traditional Danish farmhouses set around a central courtyard and Chinese architecture, in which the houses open out onto a central court but are protected from the surroundings by their outer wall.

facts.fact: Utzon worked additively, starting with one unit and growing from it while responding to the land and surroundings.
facts.quote: The development was based on Utzon's additive approach, starting modestly with one unit and proceeding from there, taking into account the lay of the land and the surroundings.

facts.fact: The invitation came from Dansk Samvirke, which wanted pensioners returning to Denmark to live together.
facts.quote: As a result of the success of the Kingo Houses, Dansk Samvirke, an organization catering to the well-being of Danish citizens who have worked for long periods abroad, invited Utzon to develop a housing estate where pensioners returning to Denmark could live together and share their experiences.

facts.fact: The complex has courtyard homes and terraced houses around a square, with a central building holding a restaurant, meeting rooms and guest rooms.
facts.quote: Partly inspired by housing in Beijing's Forbidden City, the complex consists of 47 courtyard homes and 30 terraced houses as well as a central building with a restaurant, meeting rooms and nine guest rooms.

facts.fact: Because the site slopes and the houses face south-east or south-west, they get plenty of light and an open feel while staying private.
facts.quote: As the houses are on a slope, they all benefit from plenty of light, especially as they face either south-east or south-west.

facts.fact: The additive approach influenced later housing around Copenhagen, including Bjarke Ingels Group's Mountain Dwellings.
facts.quote: Utzon's additive architecture approach to modern housing exerted a considerable influence on subsequent developments.

facts.fact: Cocoa House was originally called Ìlé Àwọn Àgbẹ̀ ('House of Farmers') and was proposed by Obafemi Awolowo as part of the Western Region Development Plan.
facts.quote: Cocoa House (originally named Ìlé Àwọn Àgbẹ̀, or "House of Farmers") is a skyscraper in Nigeria. It was initiated by Chief Obafemi Awolowo in the late 1950s as part of the Western Region Development Plan (1955–1960); and completed in July 1964 and commissioned in July 1965, by the government of Western Region, headed by Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola.

facts.fact: It was the first skyscraper in West Africa and, from 1965 to 1979, the tallest building in Nigeria.
facts.quote: At a height of 105 metres (344 ft), it was the first skyscraper in West Africa, and was, from 1965 to 1979, the tallest building in Nigeria.

facts.fact: It was financed from the proceeds of the Western Region's agricultural exports such as cocoa, rubber and timber.
facts.quote: It was built from proceeds of agricultural commodities (e.g., cocoa, rubber, timber) of the then Western State of Nigeria.

facts.fact: The name changed to Cocoa House because it was built with cocoa export proceeds and a cocoa tree was planted in front of it.
facts.quote: The name was later changed to Cocoa House because it was built with proceeds from cocoa exportation and also because there was a cocoa tree planted in front of the building just beside a water fountain.

facts.fact: It stands in Dugbe, a major commercial area of Ibadan.
facts.quote: It is located in Dugbe, a major commercial area in Ibadan, Oyo State, Nigeria.

facts.fact: Fire gutted the whole building in January 1985 and it was renovated and reopened for commercial use in 1992.
facts.quote: The entire building was gutted by fire on January 9, 1985, which began in the top floors from malfunctioning electrical equipment. It was closed from public use until it was renovated in August 1992 and re-opened for commercial use.

facts.fact: Today it houses offices, broadcasters and the Odua Museum and Hall of Fame.
facts.quote: The building today houses offices for major firms and broadcasting companies.

facts.fact: BedZED is a housing development in Hackbridge, London, designed to create zero carbon emissions.
facts.quote: Beddington Zero Energy Development (BedZED) is an environmentally friendly housing development in Hackbridge, London, England.

facts.fact: Bill Dunster designed BedZED to be carbon neutral.
facts.quote: BedZED was designed by the architect Bill Dunster to be carbon neutral.

facts.fact: A local authority sold the land below market value so sustainable development could be economically viable, a first for a construction project.
facts.quote: The project was the first construction project where a local authority sold land at below market value to make sustainable development economically viable.

facts.fact: It was built between 2000 and 2002 and shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2003.
facts.quote: The 82 homes and 1,405 square metres (15,120 ft2) of work space was built within the period of 2000–2002. The project was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2003.

facts.fact: Monitoring found electricity use 25% below the UK average, with 11% of it produced by solar panels.
facts.quote: The electrical power used, at 3 kilowatt hours per person per day, was 25% less than the UK average; 11% of this was produced by solar panels.

facts.fact: A later review found failures, including that the 'Living Machine' water recycling facility could not clean the water sufficiently.
facts.quote: The 'Living Machine' water recycling facility had been unable to clean the water sufficiently.

facts.fact: The RIBA Journal sustainability award judges said BedZED challenges both the way we live and work.
facts.quote: 2003 – RIBA journal sustainability award – the judges said "BedZED goes way beyond the standard environmental checklist by challenging both the way we live and work... Until now, pioneering communities have often been attained at the expense of architectural ambition but at BedZED the architects have been highly innovative."

facts.fact: The school in Winnetka, Illinois was designed jointly by Perkins, Wheeler & Will with Eliel and Eero Saarinen, and opened in 1940-41.
facts.quote: The building was designed jointly by the Chicago firm of Perkins, Wheeler and Will, along with Eliel and Eero Saarinen. It currently serves kindergarten through fourth grade students. The school was established in 1940-41.

facts.fact: It is significant for its progressive educational philosophy and its International Style architecture.
facts.quote: It is significant for its progressive philosophy and its International Style architecture.

facts.fact: The architects interviewed students and teachers and sat in on classes before designing it.
facts.quote: They interviewed students and teachers about the project and sat in on classes.

facts.fact: The site was a high spot in the Skokie Marsh, filled with landfill from two Works Progress Administration projects.
facts.quote: A site for the school was selected on Crow Island, a high spot in the Skokie Marsh bordering the Crow Island Woods. The swamp was filled with landfill from two Works Progress Administration projects in the area: the Skokie Lagoons Project and a track depression for the Chicago and North Western Railway.

facts.fact: Four wings radiate from a central building with common rooms, so every classroom has its own outdoor courtyard.
facts.quote: The school has four wings emerging from a central building with common rooms. This design allows each classroom to have its own outdoor courtyard.

facts.fact: The building is one storey and flat apart from a chimney that acts as a 'fifth wing' stretching vertically.
facts.quote: The one-story building is flat with the exception of a 50-foot (15 m) chimney emerging from the north face, providing a "fifth wing" stretching vertically.

facts.fact: It was one of the first schools in North America designed in the International Style, and its form became a template for mid-century schools.
facts.quote: The school was one of the first to be designed in the international style of architecture in North America.

facts.fact: The AIA gave it the Twenty-five Year Award in 1971 and it became a National Historic Landmark in 1990.
facts.quote: The school was awarded the Twenty-five Year Award by the American Institute of Architects in 1971. It was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1990.

facts.fact: Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, was designed by Mick Pearce with Ove Arup and Partners and is ventilated and cooled entirely by natural means.
facts.quote: The Eastgate Centre is a shopping centre and office block in the business centre of Harare, Zimbabwe, designed by Mick Pearce and built by Ove Arup and Partners.

facts.fact: It has retail on the lower floors and offices above, in two rows lined along a glass-covered atrium and linked by skyways.
facts.quote: Eastgate contains nine storeys of commercial space lined up into two rows that ran along a glass-covered atrium, with retail shops situated on the first two floors and offices above them.

facts.fact: Brick funnels connect to each office and shop; they channel cool air from the basement and let hot air escape from the top.
facts.quote: In-between the commercial spaces there are forty-eight brick funnels connected to each office and store. Funnels channel cool air from the basement and allow hot air to escape from the top of the building.

facts.fact: Its massive concrete walls limit solar heat gain, and the masonry patterns echo the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe.
facts.quote: Its massive concrete walls work to reduce of solar-heat gain, and the patterns of the masonry are inspired by indigenous architecture of stone walls found in Great Zimbabwe, ruins of a city 200 miles southeast of Harare.

facts.fact: The passive system takes in cool night air and distributes it through the building by day.
facts.quote: Eastgate incorporates passive cooling system, which conditions the interior air temperature by harvesting cool night air and dispensing it around the interior of Eastgate during the day.

facts.fact: Pearce took inspiration from the way a termite mound keeps a constant temperature.
facts.quote: In his design Pearce was inspired by the termite mound's specific architecture that maintains a constant temperature in a "climate that fluctuates greatly between 35 degrees at night and 104 degrees during the day".

facts.fact: Arup specified sealed windows, relying on ducted ventilation, because of noise pollution and unpredictable wind pressures and temperatures.
facts.quote: They said all windows must be sealed because of noise pollution and unpredictable wind pressures and temperatures, relying on ducted ventilation.

facts.fact: Passively cooled, Eastgate is reported to use only 10% of the energy of a conventionally cooled building of similar space.
facts.quote: Passively cooled, Eastgate uses only 10% of the energy required by conventionally cooled building with similar space.

facts.fact: Eastgate is described as a forerunner of green building in sub-Saharan Africa and is emulated by London's Portcullis House.
facts.quote: The construction of Eastgate, Zimbabwe became the "forerunner in incorporating green building technologies in the sub-Saharan Africa".

facts.fact: The National Center for Atmospheric Research laboratory in Boulder, Colorado, was designed by I. M. Pei, his first project outside city building design.
facts.quote: The building complex was designed by modernist architect I. M. Pei in 1961 as his first project outside of city building design.

facts.fact: It is noted for Anasazi-inspired architecture and bush-hammered concrete that blends into the surrounding landscape.
facts.quote: It has been noted for its Anasazi-inspired architecture and use of bush-hammered concrete to blend into the surrounding area.

facts.fact: The laboratory site is the Table Mesa below the Flatirons sandstone cliffs.
facts.quote: In 1960 the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) appointed Walter Orr Roberts as the founding director of the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and designated the Table Mesa below the Flatirons sandstone cliffs as its laboratory site.

facts.fact: Pei revised the design from a single tall tower to a village-like group of three towers, and built it in two phases to fit a budget set by the National Science Foundation.
facts.quote: Through his revisions he moved from a single tall tower concept to a series of three 5 story towers set up in a village-like model. Also, he moved from a single stage construction to an incremental two phase approach that better suited NCAR's National Science Foundation-imposed budget constraints.

facts.fact: He based the design on the Anasazi cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, using bush-hammered concrete, geometric forms and a local pinkish aggregate to blend with the Flatirons hills.
facts.quote: Pei based his design on the Anasazi cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde. He used techniques such as bush-hammering the concrete, laying out geometric shapes for the buildings, and using a local pinkish aggregate to help the complex blend in with the surrounding Flatirons hills on the Table Mesa.

facts.fact: The plan is laid out in a maze-like fashion to encourage interaction among scientists.
facts.quote: He also laid out the building in a maze-like fashion to encourage greater interaction among the scientists.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1966 and dedicated in 1967 and remains the primary NCAR laboratory, despite leaky roofs and personnel flow problems.
facts.quote: The building was completed in 1966 and dedicated in 1967. Despite problems with leaky roofs and personnel flow, the building was considered a success in the scientific and architectural communities and, as of 2009, remains the primary NCAR laboratory.

facts.fact: The American Institute of Architects Colorado chapter gave it a 25 Year Award, for buildings that withstand the test of time.
facts.quote: The lab won the 1967 Laboratory of the Year award by Industrial Research Magazine and the 1997 American Institute of Architects: Colorado Chapter's 25 Year Award. The latter award is given for buildings that continue to serve their original function and have withstood the "test of time" over a 25- to 35-year period.

facts.fact: Morphosis and Thomas Blurock Architects designed the school in an expressionist modern style, led by Thom Mayne of Morphosis.
facts.quote: The school was designed in an expressionist modern style by Morphosis and Thomas Blurock Architects, led by architect Thom Mayne of Morphosis.

facts.fact: It is built on a steep hillside on land previously considered unusable.
facts.quote: It is situated on a steep hillside on land previously considered unusable.

facts.fact: Its design is the subject of the book Morphosis/Diamond Ranch High School.
facts.quote: The school's unique architectural design was recognized in the book Morphosis/Diamond Ranch High School.

facts.fact: In 1991 voters approved a school bond that included money designated for Diamond Ranch.
facts.quote: June 1991 – PUSD voters approved a $62.5 million general obligation bond to improve school facilities district-wide, including approximately $10 million designated for Diamond Ranch.

facts.fact: The school district hired Morphosis in November 1993.
facts.quote: November 1993 – The school district hires Morphosis to design the school.

facts.fact: The school officially opened to students in September 1997 while construction continued.
facts.quote: September 5, 1997 – DRHS was officially opened for students, while construction continues.

facts.fact: Because of its modernist architecture, size and location the school has appeared in several films and commercials.
facts.quote: Because of its modernist architecture, size and location in California, the school has appeared in movies such as The Cell, Orange County, Serenity, Live Free or Die Hard, and The Thinning.

facts.fact: The building was originally the Chiat/Day Building, built in 1991 for an advertising agency and designed by Frank Gehry.
facts.quote: Originally known as the Chiat/Day Building, it was built in 1991 for the advertising agency Chiat/Day (now TBWA\Chiat\Day) and designed by architect Frank Gehry.

facts.fact: A public artwork, Giant Binoculars by Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen, sits on the street-facing facade and gives the building its popular name.
facts.quote: The building has a prominent public artwork entitled Giant Binoculars (1991), designed by artists Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen, on its street-facing façade, hence the vernacular name.

facts.fact: The sculpture covers both a car and pedestrian entrance, with the garage entrance between the two telescopes.
facts.quote: The Giant Binoculars sculpture covers both a car and pedestrian entrance; the entrance to the parking garage is between the two telescopes of the binoculars.

facts.fact: Construction was delayed for a few years after hazardous materials were found on the site.
facts.quote: The 75,000-square-foot (7,000 m2) building was delayed for a few years after hazardous materials were found on the building site, requiring removal.

facts.fact: Google became the tenant in 2011 and added two neighbouring buildings.
facts.quote: The latest tenant of this building was Google in 2011, which added two neighboring buildings as part of a major expansion to establish a larger employment presence in Los Angeles.

facts.fact: Jonas Salk and Louis Kahn asked the city of San Diego for land on the Torrey Pines Mesa in March 1960 and were granted it after a referendum in June 1960.
facts.quote: Salk and architect Louis I. Kahn approached the city of San Diego in March 1960 about a gift of land on the Torrey Pines Mesa and were granted their request after a referendum in June 1960.

facts.fact: The campus was meant to have three clusters (meetings, living quarters and laboratories), but only the laboratories were built: two parallel blocks enclosing a water garden.
facts.quote: The Salk Institute, La Jolla, California (1959–1965) was to be a campus composed of three clusters: meeting and conference areas, living quarters, and laboratories. Only the laboratory cluster, consisting of two parallel blocks enclosing a water garden, was built.

facts.fact: The two laboratory blocks frame a long view of the Pacific Ocean, accentuated by a thin linear fountain.
facts.quote: The two laboratory blocks frame a long view of the Pacific Ocean, accentuated by a thin linear fountain that seems to reach for the horizon.

facts.fact: Salk wanted a beautiful campus to attract the best researchers in the world.
facts.quote: The campus was designed by Louis Kahn. Salk had sought a beautiful campus in order to draw the best researchers in the world.

facts.fact: The two symmetric wings flank a travertine-paved central plaza with a water stream running towards the ocean.
facts.quote: Jack MacAllister, FAIA, of the Kahn office, was the supervising architect and a design influence on the building that consists of two symmetric wings with a water stream flowing towards the ocean in the middle travertine-paved central plaza that separates the two.

facts.fact: There are no walls separating laboratories on any floor, to promote collaboration.
facts.quote: The buildings themselves have been designed to promote collaboration, and thus there are no walls separating laboratories on any of the floors.

facts.fact: After two years of design, Kahn and the Institute changed the plan from four narrow laboratory buildings to two wider ones, and from two floors to three.
facts.quote: After two years of design work, and after the design had been approved and meetings with building contractors had begun, Kahn and the Salk Institute abruptly decided to reduce the number of laboratory buildings from four narrow ones to two wider ones and to increase the number of floors per building from two to three.

facts.fact: Engineer August Komendant re-engineered the structure and trained construction workers to produce a highly refined concrete finish.
facts.quote: August Komendant re-engineered the structure and produced a new set of drawings with a speed that professor Leslie described as "legendary". Komendant also trained the construction workers in techniques for producing a highly refined concrete finish.

facts.fact: Inside the laboratories, ducts and vents are carried by concrete Vierendeel trusses supported by post-tensioned columns.
facts.quote: Inside the laboratories, the ducts and vents are reinforced by concrete Vierendeel trusses supported by post-tensioned columns.

facts.fact: After seeing Luis Barragán's work at MoMA, Kahn invited him to collaborate on the court; Barragán advised a plaza with a single water feature and no plants.
facts.quote: When he saw an exhibit of Luis Barragan's work at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, Kahn invited Baragan to collaborate on the court that separated the two buildings. Barragan told Kahn that he should not add one leaf, nor plant, not one flower, nor dirt, instead, make it a plaza with a single water feature.

facts.fact: The concrete is said to use volcanic ash, following ancient Roman techniques, and gives a warm, pinkish glow.
facts.quote: According to A. Perez, the concrete was made with volcanic ash relying on the basis of ancient Roman concrete making techniques, and as a result gives off a warm, pinkish glow.

facts.fact: The AIA gave the building its Twenty-five Year Award in 1992.
facts.quote: In 1992 the American Institute of Architects (AIA) gave this building its prestigious Twenty-five Year Award, which is given to only one building per year.

facts.fact: The original buildings were designated a historical landmark in 1991.
facts.quote: The original buildings of the Salk Institute were designated a historical landmark in 1991.

facts.fact: The chapel in Pampulha, Belo Horizonte, was designed by Oscar Niemeyer in the organic modern style.
facts.quote: It was designed by the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer in the organic modern style.

facts.fact: It is the first listed modern architectural monument in Brazil and consists of four undulating concrete parabolas with outdoor mosaics.
facts.quote: It is the first listed modern architectural monument in Brazil and consists of four undulating concrete parabolas with outdoor mosaics.

facts.fact: Despite being completed in 1943, it was not consecrated until 1959, because church authorities prohibited Catholic services for 14 years.
facts.quote: Despite its completion in 1943 and Juscelino Kubitschek's call for its consecration, the church was not consecrated until 1959. For 14 years, the ecclesiastical authorities—led by Antonio dos Santos Cabral, the Archbishop of Belo Horizonte—prohibited the chapel from providing Catholic services.

facts.fact: Juscelino Kubitschek, then mayor of Belo Horizonte, was the patron of the project.
facts.quote: The mayor of Belo Horizonte, Juscelino Kubitschek, was the patron of the project.

facts.fact: Niemeyer abandoned slabs on columns and used a parabolic concrete vault, a form until then used only in hangars.
facts.quote: In this project, Niemeyer experimented with reinforced concrete, abandoning the architecture of slabs on columns and creating a parabolic concrete vault—a form until then only used in hangars.

facts.fact: The concrete vault serves as both the structure and the enclosure, eliminating the need for masonry.
facts.quote: The concrete vault serves as both the structure and the enclosure, eliminating the need for masonry.

facts.fact: Inside are the Stations of the Cross by Candido Portinari; outside, pastel ceramic tiles form abstract designs.
facts.quote: The interior features the Stations of the Cross, made up of 14 panels by Candido Portinari, considered one of his most characteristic works. Alfredo Ceschiatti carved the bronze bas-reliefs of the baptistery. On the exterior, the figurative art panels are by Portinari and the abstract ones are by Paulo Werneck. The exterior walls are covered in pastel ceramic tiles in shades of light blue and white, forming abstract designs.

facts.fact: Roberto Burle Marx designed the landscape.
facts.quote: The distinctive landscape of the church is the work of Roberto Burle Marx, a longtime Niemeyer collaborator.

facts.fact: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2016 as part of the Pampulha Modern Ensemble.
facts.quote: The Church of Saint Francis of Assisi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2016.

facts.fact: Giancarlo De Carlo designed the Terni neighbourhood from 1969 to 1974 to house workers of the company Società Terni Acciaierie.
facts.quote: It was designed by the anarchist architect Giancarlo De Carlo from 1969 to 1974 to house 3,000 workers from the company Società Terni Acciaierie.

facts.fact: The concrete housing complex follows New Brutalist style and is a classic example of participatory design.
facts.quote: The concrete housing complex was designed after New Brutalism style. It is known for the important role of the inhabitants in the design choices, being classified as participatory design and an example of anarchist architecture.

facts.fact: Houses differ in size and are connected by a web of stairs, corridors and gardens.
facts.quote: The houses differ in size and they are connected through a web of stairs, corridors and gardens.

facts.fact: Over a thousand people took part in meetings, interviews and debates, and exhibitions of international housing models were held to educate the community about design possibilities.
facts.quote: The community was deeply involved in the construction process through meetings, interviews and debates, with more than a thousand people involved. After two months of discussions, an exhibition was made at Galleria Poliantea in April–May 1970, with models from many parts of the world to educate the community about the design possibilities.

facts.fact: The project was De Carlo's test of his theory of popular participation in design, and a response to Carlo Aymonino's Monte Amiata housing in Milan.
facts.quote: New Matteotti Village was created as an answer of De Carlo to Carlo Aymonino's Monte Amiata Gallaratese housing complex in Milan, commissioned by Società Mineraria Monte Amiata as an investment in real estate speculation. The project served as testing grounds for De Carlo's theory of popular participation on the creation of the design.

facts.fact: De Carlo wanted to impose an overall low-rise, high-density design, while the sociologist wanted residents to help with every aspect of it.
facts.quote: De Carlo and sociologist De Mesi diverged on how the village was to be built. The architect wanted to impose an overall design of a low-rise, high-density village to the future inhabitants, while De Mesi wanted them to help with every aspect of the design.

facts.fact: The neighbourhood was only partly built: the old village's community opposed the project and, when the company's president left, construction halted for good.
facts.quote: The new neighborhood was partially built between 1969 and 1974. The community of the old village opposed the project and wanted to have the land rights. They involved the Catholic Church and the far-left group Lotta Continua (Continuous Struggle) into the conflict. Gianlupo Osti also left the presidency of the company, thus halting the construction efforts for good.

facts.fact: The Michael Lee-Chin Crystal is the centrepiece of the museum's expansion, a deconstructivist crystalline-form structure.
facts.quote: The centrepiece of the project was a deconstructivist crystalline-form structure called the Michael Lee-Chin Crystal.

facts.fact: Daniel Libeskind's design was selected from 50 finalists in an international competition.
facts.quote: The structure was created by architect Daniel Libeskind, whose design was selected from among 50 finalists in an international competition.

facts.fact: The Crystal replaced the Queen Elizabeth II Terrace Galleries and includes a new sliding-door entrance on Bloor Street; it was controversial.
facts.quote: Replacing the Queen Elizabeth II Terrace Galleries was the controversial "Michael Lee-Chin Crystal", a multimillion-dollar expansion to the museum designed by Daniel Libeskind, including a new sliding door entrance on Bloor Street, first opened in 2007.

facts.fact: The Crystal's canted walls do not touch the existing heritage buildings but close the gap between the new form and the old walls.
facts.quote: The Crystal's canted walls do not touch the sides of the existing heritage buildings but are used to close the envelope between the new form and existing walls.

facts.fact: The main lobby is a three-storey atrium, the Hyacinth Gloria Chen Crystal Court.
facts.quote: The main lobby is a three-storey high atrium, named the Hyacinth Gloria Chen Crystal Court.

facts.fact: Inside the Crystal are galleries, a restaurant lounge, a cafeteria and Canada's largest temporary exhibition hall in a museum.
facts.quote: Within the Crystal there is a gift shop, C5 restaurant lounge (closed until further notice), a cafeteria, seven additional galleries and Canada's largest temporary exhibition hall in a museum.

facts.fact: The design echoes other Libeskind works, notably the Jewish Museum in Berlin.
facts.quote: The building's design is similar to some of Libeskind's other works, notably the Jewish Museum in Berlin, the London Metropolitan University Graduate Centre and the Fredric C. Hamilton Building at the Denver Art Museum.

facts.fact: In October 2007 the Crystal was reported to have significant water leakage.
facts.quote: In October 2007, the Lee-Chin Crystal was reported to have suffered from significant water leakage, causing concerns for the building's resilience to weather, especially in the face of the new structure's proximate first winter.

facts.fact: Barragán lived there until his death in 1988, and the house was modified many times, acting as a laboratory for his ideas.
facts.quote: Barragán lived there until his death in 1988, and during this time the house underwent many modifications, functioning as a kind of laboratory for his ideas.

facts.fact: UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 2004 as one of the most influential and representative examples of modern Mexican architecture.
facts.quote: In 2004, it was named a World Heritage Site by UNESCO because it is one of the most influential and representative examples of modern Mexican architecture.

facts.fact: The plain street facade, with few small windows and walls only a little different from its neighbours, gives no clue to the layout inside.
facts.quote: The facades of the house align with the street and are very plain, with rough cement walls very similar in color and composition of its neighbors.

facts.fact: The house turns inward around a garden surrounded by high walls, and has been compared to an oasis shielded from urban chaos.
facts.quote: Instead, the house focuses inward, centered on a garden, which itself is surrounded by high walls except on the west.

facts.fact: Its influences are Mexican (the buildings of his youth in Jalisco, masonry and a strong division of public and private space) as well as international.
facts.quote: Most of the architectural influence on the house is Mexican but there are also international influences as well.

facts.fact: Colour draws on vibrant traditional Mexican colours, tempered by the influence of Rufino Tamayo and Jesús Reyes Ferreira.
facts.quote: His use of color is based on the vibrant colors of traditional Mexico, tempered by the artistic influences of Rufino Tamayo and in particular, Jesús Reyes Ferreira.

facts.fact: Apart from the breakfast nook, the house is designed to need no artificial light by day, with openings placed to admit as much light as possible.
facts.quote: With the exception of the breakfast nook, the house is designed to not need artificial light during the day, with windows and other openings placed to let in as much light as possible.

facts.fact: Floor levels are irregular and rooms have different heights.
facts.quote: The levels of the floors are not regular and rooms have different heights.

facts.fact: The entrance foyer is bare and dim, acting as a buffer between the interior and the outside world.
facts.quote: After entering the door at #14, one enters a bare and dim foyer, whose main purpose is that of a buffer between the interior of the house and outside world.

facts.fact: CEPT began as the School of Architecture in 1962, set up by the Ahmedabad Education Society.
facts.quote: The Centre for Environment Planning & Technology was established as the School of Architecture in 1962, by The Ahmedabad Education Society (AES), followed by the School of Planning, School of Building Science and Technology and School of Interior Design in 1972, 1982 and 1991 respectively, which were established with aid from the Ministry of Human Resource Development, the Government of Gujarat and the Ford Foundation.

facts.fact: B. V. Doshi was founding director of the School of Architecture (1962–1972).
facts.quote: B. V. Doshi - The founder Director of the School of Architecture, Ahmedabad (1962–1972), founder Director of the School of Planning (1972–1979), founder Dean of the Centre for Environmental Planning and Technology (1972–1981), founder member of the Visual Arts Centre, Ahmedabad and founder Director of the Kanoria Centre for Arts, Ahmedabad and the first Indian winner of Pritzker Prize.

facts.fact: The planning, building science and interior design schools followed in 1972, 1982 and 1991.
facts.quote: The Centre for Environment Planning & Technology was established as the School of Architecture in 1962, by The Ahmedabad Education Society (AES), followed by the School of Planning, School of Building Science and Technology and School of Interior Design in 1972, 1982 and 1991 respectively, which were established with aid from the Ministry of Human Resource Development, the Government of Gujarat and the Ford Foundation.

facts.fact: It became a university in 2005 and was renamed CEPT University in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2005 it became a university through the Centre for Environmental Planning and Technology University Act, 2005. It was renamed "CEPT University" through CEPT University Act, 2010.

facts.fact: Foster and Partners designed Bloomberg London with structural engineer AKT II, and Sir Robert McAlpine built it.
facts.quote: The building was designed by architects Foster and Partners with structural engineer AKT II, and constructed by Sir Robert McAlpine at a cost of £1bn.

facts.fact: It is two buildings divided by a covered arcade and linked by bridges.
facts.quote: It consists of two buildings, divided by a covered arcade. The buildings are linked by bridges.

facts.fact: The arcade contains restaurants and reinstates part of Watling Street, an ancient Roman road.
facts.quote: The arcade contains several restaurants, and reinstates part of Watling Street, an ancient Roman road.

facts.fact: The facade is clad in Derbyshire sandstone with bronze ventilation fins.
facts.quote: The building is clad in 9,600 tonnes of Derbyshire sandstone with bronze ventilation fins.

facts.fact: Inside, the floors are linked by custom glass lifts and a helical bronze 'ramp' that dominates the interior.
facts.quote: Inside, the floors are linked by custom glass lifts and a 210m helical bronze "ramp", which dominates the interior of the building.

facts.fact: The cores are on the outside to create a single open-plan space inside.
facts.quote: The cores of the building are on the outside, to create a single open-plan space inside.

facts.fact: The lobby is a self-supporting 'vortex' of three curved timber shells, and express lifts take visitors to a pantry on the sixth floor with a view of St Paul's Cathedral.
facts.quote: Express lifts take visitors from the lobby, a self-supporting "vortex" of three curved timber shells, to the double-height pantry on the sixth floor, with view of St Paul's Cathedral.

facts.fact: It scored 98.5% against the BREEAM sustainability assessment, the highest design-stage score for any major office development.
facts.quote: It achieved a 98.5% score against the BREEAM sustainability assessment method, the highest design-stage score ever achieved by any major office development.

facts.fact: Custom aluminium ceiling 'petals', inspired by New York pressed-metal ceilings, act as light diffusers, cooling elements and acoustic attenuation.
facts.quote: The ceilings are custom aluminium "petals", inspired by the pressed metal ceilings of New York, which act as light diffusers, cooling elements and acoustic attenuation.

facts.fact: The RIBA awarded the Stirling Prize to Bloomberg London in 2018.
facts.quote: In 2018, the RIBA awarded the Stirling Prize to Bloomberg London.

facts.fact: It has been criticised as wasteful for its specialised solutions and imported materials.
facts.quote: The design and building process of the building has been criticised as wasteful: it required developing specialised solutions not applicable anywhere else, and the construction required 600 tonnes of Japanese bronze and 10,000 tonnes of imported Indian granite, rather than using locally sourced or recycled materials.

facts.fact: The Bergpolderflat in Rotterdam was the first gallery flat in the Netherlands.
facts.quote: The Bergpolderflat in the Rotterdam district Bergpolder (corner of Abraham Kuyperlaan and Borgesiusstraat) was the first gallery flat in the Netherlands.

facts.fact: It was designed in 1933/1934 by W. van Tijen with Brinkman and Van der Vlugt, in a functional, light and airy Modern style, on a steel skeleton.
facts.quote: The flat has a steel skeleton and was designed in 1933/1934 by the architect W. de Tijen in collaboration with architects Brinkman and Van der Vlugt in the Modern style, functional, sleek, light and airy.

facts.fact: It has nine floors and 72 homes reached through an accessible gallery, with a common washroom in the basement.
facts.quote: The flat has nine floors and 72 homes through an accessible gallery.

facts.fact: The gallery with a balcony, central staircase and open glass walls is noted as first applied generally in this building.
facts.quote: In Bergpolderflat cases were first applied generally, later, as the gallery with a balcony, central staircase and open the glass walls.

facts.fact: Traditional wooden beams are combined with a fireproof three-layer concrete floor.
facts.quote: There is still the traditional wooden construction beams, but with three layers is a fireproof concrete floor.

facts.fact: Critics noted the limited number of bedrooms; the architect said the homes were designed for modern young people who like simple, light and space.
facts.quote: There was criticism of the limited number of bedrooms. de Tijen disputed such criticism by stating that "the houses were mainly designed for modern young people who like simple, light and space."

facts.fact: The building is a national monument and was renovated in 1996.
facts.quote: In 1996, the building, a national monument, was renovated by Vestia.

facts.fact: The Louvre-Lens in Lens, France, displays works lent from the Musée du Louvre and is part of an effort to give people outside Paris access to French cultural institutions.
facts.quote: The Louvre-Lens annex is part of an effort to provide access to French cultural institutions for people who live outside of Paris.

facts.fact: The site was chosen in hopes of reversing the fortunes of the depressed Lens mining community.
facts.quote: The museum site was chosen in hopes of reversing the fortunes of the depressed Lens mining community, which was devastated by both World Wars and the Nazi occupation, and suffered multiple mining catastrophes including the Courrières mine disaster in 1906, the worst in European history, and a 1974 tragedy killing 42 miners.

facts.fact: Officials took inspiration from Bilbao's transformation after the Guggenheim (the 'Bilbao effect'); some cautioned the comparison is limited, and some Lens locals found the project patronizing.
facts.quote: Officials took inspiration from the economic transformation of the Spanish industrial city of Bilbao, which was caused, in part, by the construction of the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao satellite (dubbed the "Bilbao effect", though some cautioned that the comparison is limited due to the much smaller population of Lens, and its lack of other tourist attractions.) Some Lens locals were critical of the project; they felt that the project to bring culture to their city was "patronizing".

facts.fact: A design contest was won by SANAA with Imrey Culbert, landscape architect Catherine Mosbach and museographer Studio Adrien Gardère.
facts.quote: A worldwide design contest was won by Japanese architectural firm SANAA in collaboration with New York firm Imrey Culbert, French landscape architect Catherine Mosbach, and museographer Studio Adrien Gardère.

facts.fact: The museum is built on a mining site that closed in the 1960s.
facts.quote: The museum is built on a 20-hectare (49-acre) mining site that closed in the 1960s.

facts.fact: To blend into its surroundings, the architects designed a string of five low-profile structures: a square central one with glass walls and rectangular ones with polished aluminium facades that give a blurry reflection of the surroundings.
facts.quote: To make the building blend into the surrounding area, the architects designed a string of five low-profile structures; the central one is square with glass walls and the others are rectangular with polished, aluminum facades that gave a blurry reflection of the surroundings.

facts.fact: A central building flanked by two wings mimics the Paris Louvre.
facts.quote: The design of a central building flanked by two wings mimics the Paris Louvre.

facts.fact: The Galerie du Temps arranges items from the Paris Louvre chronologically, regardless of style or country of origin.
facts.quote: To the east of the entry hall is the 3,000 m2 (32,000 sq ft) Galerie du Temps which houses approximately 200 items from the Paris Louvre collection. The items in the large, open hall are arranged chronologically, from 3,500 BC to the mid-19th century, regardless of style or country of origin.

facts.fact: Foster & Partners designed the Commerzbank headquarters in Frankfurt with Arup and Krebs & Kiefer as structural engineers.
facts.quote: Commerzbank Tower was designed by Foster & Partners, with Arup and Krebs & Kiefer (structural engineering), J. Roger Preston with P&A Petterson Ahrens (mechanical engineering), Schad & Hölzel (electrical engineering).

facts.fact: Frankfurt's Green Party encouraged the bank to build a 'green' skyscraper; the result was called the world's first so-called ecological skyscraper.
facts.quote: When the building was planned in the early 1990s, Frankfurt's Green Party, who governed the city together with the Social Democratic Party, encouraged the Commerzbank to design a 'green' skyscraper. The result was the world's first so-called ecological skyscraper: besides the use of 'sky-gardens', environmentally friendly technologies were employed to reduce energy required for heating and cooling.

facts.fact: The tower is a rounded equilateral triangle with a central triangular atrium that opens onto sky gardens at nine levels.
facts.quote: Commerzbank Tower is shaped as a 60-metre-wide (197 ft) rounded equilateral triangle with a central, triangular atrium.

facts.fact: At nine levels the atrium opens to one of the three sides, forming large sky gardens that let in natural light and reduce the need for artificial lighting.
facts.quote: At nine different levels, the atrium opens up to one of the three sides, forming large sky gardens. These open areas allow more natural light in the building, reducing the need for artificial lighting.

facts.fact: The sky gardens also give offices on the other two sides a view of either the city or the garden.
facts.quote: At the same time it ensures offices in the building's two other sides have a view of either the city or the garden.

facts.fact: To avoid supporting columns in the sky gardens the building was built in steel instead of concrete, the first skyscraper in Germany to use steel as its main construction material.
facts.quote: In order to eliminate the need of supporting columns in the sky gardens, the building was constructed in steel rather than the conventional (and cheaper) concrete. It was the first skyscraper in Germany where steel was used as the main construction material.

facts.fact: It provides office space for the Commerzbank headquarters, including winter gardens and natural lighting and air circulation.
facts.quote: The building provides 121,000 m2 (1,300,000 sq ft) of office space for the Commerzbank headquarters, including winter gardens and natural lighting and air circulation.

facts.fact: Christian de Portzamparc designed the Cité de la Musique with the nearby Conservatoire de Paris, and it opened in 1995.
facts.quote: It was designed with the nearby Conservatoire de Paris (CNSMDP) by the architect Christian de Portzamparc and opened in 1995.

facts.fact: It was part of François Mitterrand's Grands Projets and reinvented La Villette, the former slaughterhouse district.
facts.quote: Part of François Mitterrand's Grands Projets, the Cité de la Musique reinvented La Villette – the former slaughterhouse district.

facts.fact: It is a group of music institutions: an amphitheatre, a concert hall, a music museum, a library, exhibition halls and workshops.
facts.quote: It consists of an amphitheater, a concert hall that can accommodate an audience of 800–1,000, a music museum containing an important collection of music instruments from different cultural traditions, dating mainly from the fifteenth- to twentieth-century, a music library, exhibition halls and workshops.

facts.fact: In 2015 it was renamed Philharmonie 2 when Jean Nouvel's larger symphony hall was built as Philharmonie 1.
facts.quote: In 2015, it was renamed Philharmonie 2 as part of the Philharmonie de Paris when a larger symphony hall was built by Jean Nouvel and named Philharmonie 1.

facts.fact: The Musée de la Musique shows instruments from Western classical, modern and non-European music from the sixteenth century to the present.
facts.quote: The museum's collection, which opened to the public in 1864, and was relocated at the Cité de la Musique in 1997, contains instruments used in Western classical, modern and non-European music from the sixteenth century to the present time.
